title: Protocols: interfaces by shape
tasks: Switchable and Sensor: two small runtime-checkable Protocols
Speaker and MotionSensor as Devices (Blinds is given); register all three and rebuild devices
power_down(things): switch off everything Switchable, including objects that never inherit from anything
active_sensors(sensors): the sensors currently reading above zero
explanation: A Protocol describes a capability by its shape, so Light, Speaker and a vendor plug all satisfy Switchable without sharing a base class. power_down() asks each object for the capability and ignores the rest, which is what makes it work for code you do not control. Device stays an ABC because it is a family you own with shared code; Switchable and Sensor are roles that cut across families.

hints.title: Writing a Protocol
hints.content: Inherit from Protocol and write signatures with ... as the body: def turn_on(self) -> None: ... and def turn_off(self) -> None: ... Keep @runtime_checkable above the class.

hints.title: The two devices
hints.content: Speaker mirrors Light: __init__ sets playing = False and volume = 30; execute handles "on", "off" and "volume". MotionSensor has detected = False, trigger() sets it True, clear() sets it False, and read() returns 1.0 if self.detected else 0.0.

hints.title: Helpers
hints.content: power_down: loop over things, and when isinstance(thing, Switchable) call thing.turn_off() and add one to a counter, then return the counter. active_sensors is a list comprehension: [s for s in sensors if s.read() > 0]. Don't forget FACTORIES.update(...) and devices = build_devices(CATALOG).

checks.prompt: A third-party `SmartPlug` class has `turn_on()` and `turn_off()` methods but knows nothing about your code. Which statement is true?

options: It must be wrapped in a Device subclass before power_down() can use it
It already satisfies Switchable, because the Protocol only cares about its shape
It cannot be used until it inherits from Switchable
power_down() raises a TypeError for it

checks.explanation: Structural typing: `isinstance(SmartPlug(), Switchable)` is `True` because the methods exist, with no inheritance needed. That is exactly why Protocols are the right tool for libraries and test fakes.

checks.prompt: Which design choice fits an ABC better than a Protocol?

options: Accepting a fake clock in a unit test
A family of classes you own that share code and state (describe(), self.spec)
Describing a single method a third-party library already has
Letting unrelated classes opt in just by having a method

checks.explanation: ABCs shine when you control the hierarchy and want shared implementation plus an instantiation-time check. Protocols shine at the edges, where you can't or won't force inheritance.
